title: The Goan OCI Struggle: How a Bureaucratic Catch-22 Left Thousands in Limbo
excerpt: Goans who acquired Portuguese citizenship for EU access found their Indian passports revoked and their path to Overseas Citizen of India status blocked by a paperwork gap — a problem only partially resolved by a 2024 policy fix.
body:
• Thousands of Goans who acquired Portuguese citizenship have faced a bureaucratic catch-22: their Indian passports were revoked, but without a "surrender certificate" they could not apply for Overseas Citizen of India status
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs issued a directive in April 2024 allowing "revocation certificates" as an alternative to surrender certificates, opening a pathway for affected Goans to apply for OCI cards
  • The issue gained global visibility when EU Council President Antonio Costa — who has Goan ancestry — revealed his own OCI card at the India-EU trade deal signing in January 2026
  • Advocates say the fix remains incomplete, with processing delays and unclear implementation leaving many applicants in limbo

For decades, Goans have navigated a uniquely complex relationship with citizenship. As residents of a territory that was under Portuguese rule until 1961, many Goans and their descendants are eligible for Portuguese nationality under Lisbon's citizenship laws — a pathway that also grants access to the entire European Union. But exercising that right has come at a steep cost: India does not permit dual citizenship, and acquiring a Portuguese passport means losing Indian nationality.

The intended solution — the Overseas Citizen of India card, which grants foreign nationals of Indian origin the right to live and work in India indefinitely — has proven far harder to obtain than it should be. For years, a bureaucratic gap left thousands of Goans with Portuguese passports unable to apply for OCI status at all.

The Surrender Certificate Trap

The problem centered on paperwork. To apply for an OCI card, applicants needed a "surrender certificate" — a document issued when someone voluntarily gives up their Indian passport. But beginning in late 2022, the Ministry of External Affairs directed passport authorities to revoke the Indian passports of Goans who had acquired Portuguese citizenship, treating the foreign nationality as "suppressed material information." Revocation is fundamentally different from voluntary surrender, and revoked passports did not generate surrender certificates.

https://x.com/thegoanonline/status/2090636054084960467

The result was a catch-22: Goans who followed the law and disclosed their Portuguese citizenship found their Indian passports revoked — and then discovered they lacked the documentation needed to apply for OCI status. They were neither Indian citizens nor recognized overseas citizens, stuck in an administrative no-man's land.

"Obtaining an OCI when I have acted in good faith and followed all the regulations and procedures should be a formality and not a pointless battle."

— Aires Rodrigues, Goan advocate, writing from London

A Partial Fix

In April 2024, the MEA issued a new directive addressing the gap. An internal memorandum dated April 4 instructed passport-issuing authorities to issue "revocation orders" that could serve as an alternative to surrender certificates for OCI applications. The Ministry of Home Affairs agreed to accept these revocation certificates from Indian nationals "hailing from the erstwhile Portuguese territories in India, who have acquired Portuguese nationality as per Portuguese Nationality Law."

Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant welcomed the decision, thanking Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah, and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar for providing "relief to thousands of Goa citizens."

But advocates say implementation has been uneven. Processing times remain long, and some applicants report that local passport offices are still unfamiliar with the revocation certificate pathway. The 2026 OCI rule changes — including stricter digital verification, updated fee structures, and the permanent end of the older Person of Indian Origin card — have added further complexity to an already difficult process.

A High-Profile Reminder

The issue took on unexpected visibility in January 2026 when European Council President Antonio Costa, during the announcement of the India-EU trade deal in New Delhi, pulled out his own OCI card in front of Prime Minister Modi. "I am the President of the European Council, but I am also an overseas Indian citizen," Costa said, linking his Goan heritage — his father Orlando Costa was born and raised in Goa, and his grandfather lived in Margao — to the growing partnership between India and Europe.

Costa's gesture was symbolic, but it underscored a reality that thousands of ordinary Goans experience far less smoothly. Where Costa's prominent position likely eased any bureaucratic friction, many Goan families navigating the same system face months or years of delays.

What OCI Does — and Doesn't — Offer

The OCI card is often misunderstood as near-citizenship. In practice, it functions as a lifelong visa: holders can live and work in India indefinitely, own property (with some restrictions on agricultural land), and enter without separate visa applications. But they cannot vote, hold government positions, or access certain government benefits. As former diplomat and MP Shashi Tharoor has noted, "an OCI is not citizenship. It was, and remains, nothing more than a lifetime visa on a foreign passport."

"I am the President of the European Council, but I am also an overseas Indian citizen."

— Antonio Costa, EU Council President, at the India-EU trade deal signing, January 2026

For the Goan diaspora — spread across Portugal, the U.K., the Gulf states, East Africa, and beyond — the OCI card represents the primary legal mechanism for maintaining a connection to their homeland. Resolving the bureaucratic obstacles that continue to delay and deny applications remains a pressing concern for a community whose roots in India stretch back centuries.
nri_angle: Goan diaspora across Portugal, UK, Gulf states, and East Africa face ongoing obstacles to OCI status despite policy fixes; relevant to all NRIs navigating India's overseas citizenship framework
